levels.21.title: Diagnosis
levels.21.intro: Welcome to the final challenge. There are no more step-by-step instructions. This Compton scattering diagram has two mistakes.
levels.21.steps.fix.prompt: Fix the diagram so that it's a valid contribution to e⁻γ → e⁻γ. You can flip, delete and redraw the editable lines.
levels.21.steps.fix.hints.0: Check the QED rule at each vertex: one photon, one arrow coming in and one going out.
levels.21.steps.fix.hints.1: The bottom exit must be a photon, and the internal arrow must go from left to right.
levels.21.success: Perfect diagnosis. You've repaired a diagram without help.
levels.21.explanation.intuitive: First you find which rule is broken, then you fix it: that's how you debug any system.
levels.21.explanation.scientific: The corrected diagram is the s-channel contribution to Compton scattering. The internal arrow continues the flow of the incoming electron, and each vertex has exactly one photon.
levels.21.explanation.math: 𝓜_s ∝ e² ε*_ν(k′) ū(p′) γ^ν [(p̸ + k̸ + m)/((p + k)² − m²)] γ^μ u(p) ε_μ(k).
levels.22.title: Light becoming matter
levels.22.intro: Two photons collide and, from pure light, an electron and a positron are born. Build it without help.
levels.22.steps.build.prompt: Build a tree-level diagram for γγ → e⁻e⁺.
levels.22.steps.build.hints.0: Each initial photon goes to a different vertex.
levels.22.steps.build.hints.1: The electron leaves the top vertex, the positron “comes into” the bottom one (arrow toward the vertex) and a virtual electron joins the vertices.
levels.22.steps.amplitude.prompt: Your diagram has two vertices. To what power of the charge e is its amplitude 𝓜 proportional?
levels.22.steps.amplitude.options.e2.fee: One factor of e per vertex.
levels.22.steps.amplitude.options.e4.fee: That's the order of the probability, which goes as |𝓜|².
levels.22.steps.amplitude.hints.0: Each vertex contributes a factor e.
levels.22.steps.probability.prompt: The probability of the process is proportional to |𝓜|². What is it proportional to?
levels.22.steps.probability.options.e4.f: With α ≈ 1/137, each extra pair of vertices suppresses the probability about 137 times. That's why perturbation theory works.
levels.22.steps.probability.hints.1: The fine-structure constant is α = e²/(4πε₀ħc) ≈ 1/137.
levels.22.success: You've created matter from light and worked out its perturbative order.
levels.22.explanation.intuitive: The energy of light can turn into matter and antimatter: E = mc² in action.
levels.22.explanation.scientific: It's the Breit–Wheeler process (γγ → e⁻e⁺), the crossing of annihilation into two photons. It has two tree-level diagrams (t and u channels). It needs photons with enough total energy to create two electron masses.
levels.22.explanation.math: σ ∝ α² · f(s/m²). Each extra order of perturbation theory (two more vertices, with a loop) contributes a factor α ≈ 1/137.
levels.23.title: The verdict
levels.23.intro: Three candidates for contributing to Bhabha scattering (e⁻e⁺ → e⁻e⁺). One of them is an impostor.
levels.23.steps.impostor.prompt: Which one is NOT a valid contribution to e⁻e⁺ → e⁻e⁺?
levels.23.steps.impostor.options.A.feedb: A is the s channel, annihilation: it's valid.
levels.23.steps.impostor.options.B.feedb: B is the t channel, scattering: it's valid.
levels.23.steps.impostor.options.C.feedb: In C, the initial electron and the final positron share a vertex and the arrows don't flow.
levels.23.steps.impostor.hints.0: Check the arrows at each vertex of each candidate.
levels.23.steps.impostor.hints.1: Look for a vertex that two arrows arrive at.
levels.23.steps.where.prompt: Tap a vertex of the impostor where the QED rule breaks.
levels.23.steps.where.wrongDefault: That point is an external particle. Look for the vertices.
levels.23.steps.where.hints.0: In this case, both vertices fail.
levels.23.steps.where.hints.1: Two arrows come into the top one; two go out of the bottom one.
levels.23.steps.where.solved: That's where it fails: at a vertex, one arrow must come in and another go out. Charge isn't conserved.
levels.23.success: You've judged diagrams like a physicist: with the rules, not with visual intuition.
levels.23.explanation.intuitive: A drawing can look reasonable and be forbidden. The rules never fail.
levels.23.explanation.scientific: For e⁻e⁺ → e⁻e⁺, the “u” pairing joins the initial e⁻ with the final e⁺. The incoming e⁻ brings charge −1 to the vertex and the outgoing e⁺ takes away +1, so the internal line would have to carry charge −2. A photon is neutral, so that diagram doesn't exist. Visually, two arrows come into the same vertex.
levels.23.explanation.math: Current conservation at each vertex cancels any term of this kind in the perturbative expansion: only 𝓜_s and 𝓜_t contribute.
levels.24.title: Grand finale: complete Møller
levels.24.intro: A particle physics student's final exam: write down every tree-level diagram for electron–electron scattering and say how they combine.
levels.24.steps.t.hints.0: 1 and 3 share a vertex; 2 and 4, the other.
levels.24.steps.u.prompt: Now the crossed contribution, the u channel: 1 → 4 and 2 → 3.
levels.24.steps.u.hints.0: The lines will have to cross.
levels.24.steps.u.hints.1: 1 and 4 to the top vertex; 2 and 3 to the bottom one.
levels.24.steps.sign.prompt: To get the total amplitude you have to combine the two diagrams. Since electrons are identical fermions, how do they combine?
levels.24.steps.sign.diagrams.0.label: t
levels.24.steps.sign.diagrams.1.label: u
levels.24.steps.sign.options.minus.text: Their amplitudes are subtracted: 𝓜 = 𝓜_t − 𝓜_u
levels.24.steps.sign.options.minus.feedb: Swapping two identical fermions changes the sign of the amplitude (Pauli exclusion principle).
levels.24.steps.sign.options.probs.feedb: In quantum mechanics amplitudes are added, not probabilities, and that's why interference appears.
levels.24.steps.sign.options.simple.feed: Both are equally simple (two vertices) and contribute at the same order e².
levels.24.steps.sign.hints.0: In quantum mechanics, amplitudes are added, not probabilities.
levels.24.success: You've mastered tree level: you read, build and judge Feynman diagrams. Now the real thing begins: more vertices and quantum loops.
levels.24.explanation.intuitive: Two indistinguishable stories produce the same final result, and nature combines them with a minus sign that comes from the very nature of electrons.
levels.24.explanation.scientific: The tree-level Møller amplitude is the difference of the t and u channels. The interference between them is a measurable prediction, confirmed by experiment, and a direct consequence of the Pauli principle.
levels.24.explanation.math: 𝓜 = e² { [ū₃γ^μu₁][ū₄γ_μu₂]/t − [ū₄γ^μu₁][ū₃γ_μu₂]/u }, with t = (p₁ − p₃)² and u = (p₁ − p₄)².
